sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is nearly complete and preserved in three dimensions. It includes parts of the skull, a lower jaw, and some body bones. This single known specimen provides most of what scientists know about this animal.
Features in the back of the skull support placing Piscogavialis in the family Gavialidae, the group of long-snouted crocodilians.
Fossils of Piscogavialis were discovered in 1998 in the Pisco Formation of the Sacaco Basin in southern Peru. The genus Piscogavialis was described by Kraus in 1998.
Piscogavialis belongs to the family Gavialidae and is classified within the subfamily Gryposuchinae.
A 2007 phylogenetic analysis placed Piscogavialis within the subfamily Gryposuchinae alongside Aktiogavialis, Gryposuchus, Ikanogavialis, and Siquisiquesuchus.
A 2022 study depicts Piscogavialis as a more derived member of the family Gavialidae.
Piscogavialis lived from the Burdigalian to the Zanclean stages, approximately 20.45 to 3.6 million years ago.
Its fossil range spans the Miocene epochs of Huayqueriense and Montehermosense within the Pisco Formation of the Sacaco Basin in southern Peru.
Strata suggest it inhabited a coastal environment when the Pisco Basin was covered by shallow marine waters connected to the open ocean during the Miocene.
While the strata containing its remains indicate a coastal life, other related gryposuchines have been found in deposits that were clearly freshwater environments.
The extinction of Peru's marine gavialids, including Piscogavialis, was caused by dropping sea levels, the uplifting of the Andes Mountains, and falling global temperatures during the Pliocene.
A 2018 study suggests that Gryposuchinae, including Piscogavialis, may be paraphyletic and represent an evolutionary grade leading to Gavialis and the gharial.
